extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and media scholars interested in media criticism and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Use Boorstin's concept of 'pseudo-events' to identify and evaluate press releases and political publicity efforts as contrived spectacles that substitute for spontaneous news. The rubric helps spot features that make a press release a manufactured event and understand its effects on public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-events are contrivances of politicians and news corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans mistake certain "pseudo-events" for real news, when in fact they are the contrivances of politicians and news corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat press releases and similar staged happenings as manufactured content created to look like news rather than organically occurring events; evaluate authenticity by asking who organized the event and whether it was created primarily for media consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-events are political spectacles organized to tell a certain narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Pseudo-events are political spectacles (usually) organized by politicians to tell a certain narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the event/press release is designed to communicate a prepackaged story or image (rather than to report an unplanned fact). Examples given: ribbon-cuttings, presidential turkey pardons, and orchestrated press releases. If the primary goal is narrative framing, classify it as a pseudo-event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press releases are a common form of pseudo-event
rubrics_metrics.description: Most commonly, a politician might organize a press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a press release, consider that it may be the vehicle for staging an otherwise unremarkable occurrence into news; examine language, timing, and orchestration to judge whether it's meant as publicity rather than substantive reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-events fill the demand gap created by scarce naturally occurring news
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans have 'extravagant expectations' when it comes to their news consumption... Truly important, naturally occurring news stories, however, do not occur regularly or predictably—there may be droughts of newsworthy stories. In order to 'fill the gap,' news corporations report what Boorstin calls 'pseudo-events.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to evaluate motive and timing: determine whether a press release was produced to supply continuous content/entertainment for audiences and news outlets rather than to report new, independently significant developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-events are often mistaken for real news and mislead audiences about political activity
rubrics_metrics.description: These pseudo-events... are often mistaken for real news. And, more importantly, the media consumers seeing these pseudo-events often mistakenly believe these politicians are engaging 'in politics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audience perception effects: does the press release create an illusion of political action or accomplishment? Evaluate whether coverage of the release substitutes for scrutiny of actual policy or substantive political work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press-driven image-making turns leaders into 'media stars' (celebrity as 'well-knownness')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Image is also well-known for defining a celebrity as 'a person who is known for his well-knownness.' Boorstin argued that in the 1960s leaders were beginning to resemble 'media stars' rather than politicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge press releases by their role in cultivating persona and fame: consider whether the release prioritizes visibility, style, or image over policy content, thereby contributing to celebrity-style leadership rather than substantive governance.
